title: The Ghost Weaver of Kaithady: Jaffna's Loom of Dread
description:
In the arid northern lands of Jaffna, nestled among the Palmyra trees, lies Kaithady – a village once famed for its master weavers. But time, and other things, have left it quiet. They say, however, that one loom still works, long after its weaver drew her last breath.

This episode of Ceylon Dread delves into a haunting piece of Sri Lankan folklore from Jaffna, recounting the unsettling tale of Selvi, the last master weaver of Kaithady, whose spirit is said to continue her craft, weaving a destined shroud for those about to pass. This story is a dramatised retelling of local legend.
fiction_note: Based on Sri Lankan folklore; characters and events are dramatised.

scenes.narration: Have you ever felt the weight of an old village, where every dust-laden brick seems to hold a secret? That’s how Kaithady felt to Kavi, the first time he arrived. He was a young man, a bit of a skeptic, here to document the dying art of traditional weaving, if any remained. The red earth roads, the heat shimmering off the Palmyra trees, the distant hum of the lagoon… it all felt ancient. His tuk-tuk driver, an old man named Appu, pointed to a crumbling stone building, half-hidden by overgrown shrubs. “That,” Appu said, his voice dropping, “was Selvi’s workshop. The last master weaver.”
visuals: Wide shot of a dusty red-earth road in Kaithady village, Palmyra trees lining the path, a single tuk-tuk driving away into the distance under a hazy afternoon sun, 50mm lens.
Detail shot of an old, crumbling stone building, partially obscured by dry, thorny shrubs, a rusted sign just visible, golden hour light, 85mm lens.

scenes.narration: Kavi rented a small room near the village temple, where the scent of jasmine and burning incense mingled with the dry air. The first few nights were quiet. He'd sit by his kerosene lamp, sketching notes, sipping strong Ceylon tea. Then, on the third night, a sound drifted in through his open window. A rhythmic clack-thump… clack-thump. It was faint, almost like a heartbeat in the distance. He paused, pencil hovering over paper. Just the wind, he told himself, or a loose shutter in the old guesthouse. Kaithady was full of old, creaking things, after all.
visuals: Overhead shot of Kavi sitting at a rustic wooden table by a window, sketching in a notebook, a kerosene lamp casting warm light, a cup of tea beside him, dark interior, 28mm lens.
Detail shot of a slightly open wooden window frame, a thin curtain gently swaying, moonlight filtering into a dark room, focus on the textured wood, 100mm macro lens.

scenes.narration: But the sound returned the next night, clearer this time. A distinct, steady rhythm. Clack-thump, clack-thump, clack-thump. It was too regular for the wind. Too purposeful. He got up, walked to the window, and peered out into the moonlit darkness. Nothing. Just the shadows of the Palmyra swaying. The next morning, over breakfast at Amma’s small shop, he casually asked about any old workshops still in use. Amma, a woman with eyes that had seen many seasons, paused, her hand hovering over a plate of steaming idli. “The sound you hear,” she said slowly, “that is Selvi’s loom.”
visuals: Wide shot of a moonlit Kaithady village street at night, shadows of Palmyra trees stretching across dusty ground, empty except for a distant light, 35mm lens.
Close-up, over-the-shoulder shot of Amma's hands serving idli, her face partially obscured but showing a thoughtful expression, warm morning light, 50mm lens.

scenes.narration: “Selvi was the finest weaver Kaithady ever knew,” Amma continued, her voice soft, like rustling dry leaves. “Her patterns, they were like poems. Each thread, a word. And her specialty… the shrouds. Not for the living, mind you. For the departing. They say, when someone’s time was near, Selvi would know. And she would begin to weave their final covering. No one knew how. She just… knew. And now, they say, her spirit still tends her loom. Weaving. For those whose journey is about to end.” A shiver ran down Kavi’s spine, despite the morning heat.
visuals: Profile shot of an old woman, Amma, seated on a low stool on a shaded porch, her gaze distant, telling a story, soft morning light, 85mm lens.
Detail shot of very old, gnarled hands, perhaps holding a worn, intricate piece of woven fabric, dappled sunlight, shallow depth of field, 100mm macro lens.

scenes.narration: Kavi tried to dismiss it as old village superstition. A comforting story for a forgotten craft. But the clack-thump, clack-thump… it played in his mind all day. That night, as the moon rose, casting long, sharp shadows, he couldn't resist. He grabbed his small torch and stepped out. The sound was there, faint at first, then growing stronger as he walked down the narrow, unlit path, past silent homes. He knew where he was going. Towards the crumbling workshop Appu had pointed out. The air grew heavy, thick with the scent of dry earth and something else… something ancient and still.
visuals: Kavi's silhouette walking down a narrow, unpaved red-earth path at night, moon high, casting long shadows, a faint light from his small torch, 35mm film grain, 50mm lens.
Ground-level shot looking up at the overhanging branches of a Palmyra tree, moonlight filtering through, creating a dappled effect on the dusty path below, 28mm lens.

scenes.narration: The workshop stood silent under the moonlight, a dark, hulking shape. No light from within. But the sound… it was loud now. Unmistakable. Clack-thump, clack-thump. It seemed to come from the very stone walls. Kavi’s heart hammered against his ribs. He pushed at the heavy wooden door. It creaked open slowly, protesting, revealing an inky darkness inside. The air was thick with dust and the smell of old wood, old fibres. And then he saw it. In the center of the room, illuminated by a single, narrow shaft of moonlight filtering through a gap in the roof.
visuals: Wide shot of the dilapidated weaving workshop at night, its heavy wooden door slightly ajar, a sliver of darkness visible, moonbeams reflecting off a dusty patch of ground, 24mm lens.
Detail shot of the heavy, weathered wooden door of the workshop, rusted iron hinges, a faint creaking motion suggested, focus on texture and age, 85mm lens.

scenes.narration: The loom. An ancient wooden contraption, still and silent, yet… it wasn't. The shuttle moved, gliding back and forth with a soft, rhythmic clack. The threads, stretched taut, shifted and interlaced, as if guided by invisible hands. No one was there. Not a soul. Just the loom, weaving, on its own. Kavi felt a cold sweat break out on his forehead. This was impossible. Yet, it was happening. He watched, mesmerised and terrified, as a pattern slowly emerged from the interlocked threads, taking shape on the fabric.
visuals: Interior shot of the dilapidated workshop, a lone ancient wooden loom in the center, bathed in a narrow shaft of moonlight from a hole in the roof, threads visibly moving, no one present, 35mm film, long exposure.
Close-up detail of the wooden shuttle on the loom, blurred as if in motion, threads weaving themselves into a complex pattern, dust motes visible in the moonlight, 100mm macro lens.

scenes.narration: He took a hesitant step closer. The pattern was intricate, unlike anything he had ever seen. A delicate border, a central motif… familiar somehow, in a way that made his stomach clench. It was a shroud, undeniably. Made of the finest cotton, woven with such care. But the detail… a small, almost hidden symbol. A tiny, three-petaled flower, repeated at intervals. His breath hitched. He knew that symbol. It was unique to his own family, a small crest they used in heirlooms. His grandmother had one on her wedding sari. A chilling dread washed over him.
visuals: Over-the-shoulder shot of Kavi, his hand hesitantly reaching towards the fabric on the loom, back to the viewer, the loom glowing faintly in moonlight, 50mm lens.
Extreme close-up of a small, intricate woven symbol on the fabric, illuminated by a sliver of moonlight, revealing fine detail and texture, shallow depth of field, 200mm macro lens.

scenes.narration: Kavi stumbled back, tripping over a loose floorboard. The sound of the loom… it stopped. Abruptly. The shuttle froze mid-air. The threads hung still. The silence that followed was heavier, more terrifying than any sound. He felt a presence, cold and ancient, watching him. He didn’t wait. He turned and ran, scrambling through the darkness, the broken door swinging shut behind him with a low, mournful groan. He ran until his lungs burned, not daring to look back, the image of that woven flower seared into his mind.
visuals: Kavi's silhouette running away from the workshop through a dark, overgrown path, moonlight dappling through trees, creating a sense of urgency, 35mm lens.
Wide shot of the workshop door, now completely closed, appearing dark and ominous under the moon, a single distant light from the village, 50mm lens.

scenes.narration: The next morning, Kavi sat with Amma again, shaken, recounting his experience in a hushed voice. Amma listened, her face grave, occasionally nodding slowly. When he finished, she looked at him, her eyes holding a deep, ancient sadness. “The symbol,” she said softly. “The three-petaled flower… I have seen it before. Selvi wove it only for those whose family line was old, whose roots ran deep in this land. And for them, her shroud was a blessing. Or a warning. It depended on how you saw it.”
visuals: Profile shot of Kavi and Amma seated on a simple wooden bench on a shaded porch, Kavi looking troubled, Amma listening intently, morning light, 85mm lens.
Close-up of Amma's face, her expression one of deep contemplation and understanding, lines etched by time, soft morning light, 100mm lens.

scenes.narration: Kavi left Kaithady that afternoon. The memory of the loom, the self-moving threads, the silence, and that single, familiar symbol on the shroud… it clung to him like the red dust of the village. He never learned whose name the shroud was truly meant for. His grandmother lived many more years. But sometimes, in the dead of night, he still hears it. That faint, rhythmic clack-thump, clack-thump. A reminder that some threads, once woven, can never be undone. And some stories, once started, never truly end. Only linger, in the quiet corners of the world.
visuals: Wide shot of a tuk-tuk driving away down a long, dusty red-earth road, leaving Kaithady village behind, under a vast, pale afternoon sky, 28mm lens.
Distant, atmospheric shot of the abandoned workshop, almost hidden by overgrown foliage, under a fading moon in the pre-dawn light, evoking a sense of enduring mystery, 135mm lens.

shorts.title: The Loom That Weaves for the Dead: Kaithady's Secret
shorts.narration: The first time Kavi heard it, he dismissed it. A faint clack-thump, clack-thump, drifting through his window in the quiet Jaffna village of Kaithady. Just the wind, he thought, or an old house settling. But the sound returned. Clearer. Too rhythmic for the wind. Too purposeful. It was a loom, weaving. In a village where the last weaver, Selvi, had died decades ago. Locals whispered that Selvi’s spirit still worked her loom, weaving shrouds for those whose time was near. Skeptical, Kavi decided to investigate. That night, under a full moon, he walked towards the abandoned workshop. The sound grew louder with every step. Clack-thump, clack-thump. He pushed the heavy, creaking door open, revealing an inky darkness inside. The full story is on our channel.
